title: Of the uncertainty of our judgment
paragraphs: Well said is this line:
["There is everywhere much liberty of speech."--Iliad, xx. 249.]
For example:
["Hannibal conquered, but knew not how to make the best use of his victorious venture."--Petrarch, Son., 83.]

Anyone wanting to develop this point — to condemn our commanders' failure to press home the victory at Moncontour, or to accuse the King of Spain of not knowing how to make the most of his advantage over us at St. Quentin — may put these lapses down to a soul already drunk with success, or to a spirit so full and overstuffed with the start of good fortune that it has lost the appetite for adding to it, having quite enough on its plate to digest what it has already swallowed. He has his arms full and can hold no more; he is unworthy of the benefit fortune has handed him and of the advantage she has placed in his hand. For what good does it do him if he nonetheless gives his enemy time to regroup and rally? What chance is there that he will dare another day to attack an enemy reunited, reorganised, and freshly armed with anger and revenge — when he did not dare pursue them while they were routed and unmanned by fear?
"Dum fortuna calet, dum conficit omnia terror."
["Whilst fortune is fresh, and terror finishes all."--Lucan, vii. 734.]

But for all that, what better chance can he expect than the one he has thrown away? This is not fencing, where the most hits wins the prize; for as long as the enemy is on his feet, the game has to start over, and a victory that does not put an end to the war is not properly a victory at all. In the engagement where Caesar came off worst, near the city of Oricum, he taunted Pompey's soldiers by saying he would have been lost had their general known how to win. He paid Pompey back in a very different way when his own turn came.

But why might one not also argue the opposite — that it is the mark of a hasty and insatiable spirit not to know how to bound and restrain its appetite; that to exceed the measure God has set on his favours is to abuse them; and that to fling yourself back into danger after a victory is to put yourself a second time at the mercy of fortune; that one of the great pieces of discretion in war is not to drive an enemy to despair? Sulla and Marius, in the Social War, after defeating the Marsians, saw a reserve body still coming on, goaded by despair like maddened beasts, and judged it not wise to take their charge. Had Monsieur de Foix's ardour not carried him so furiously after the remains of the victory at Ravenna, he would not have darkened it with his own death. And the fresh memory of his example saved Monsieur d'Anguien from the same misfortune at the battle of Serisoles. It is dangerous to press a man for whom you have left no way out except his weapons, for necessity teaches violent decisions:
"Gravissimi sunt morsus irritatae necessitatis."
["Irritated necessity bites deepest."--Portius Latro., Declam.]
"Vincitur haud gratis, jugulo qui provocat hostem."
["He is not readily beaten who provokes the enemy by shewing his throat."--or: "He who presents himself to his foe, sells his life dear."--Lucan, iv. 275.]

This is what made Pharax hold back the King of Lacedaemon, who had just won a battle against the Mantineans, from charging a thousand Argians who had escaped in a body from the defeat — better, he thought, to let them slip off freely than to meet valour sharpened and enraged by misfortune. Clodomir, king of Aquitaine, after his victory pursued Gondemar, king of Burgundy, who was beaten and making off as fast as he could for safety; he forced him to turn and face him, and that stubbornness cost Clodomir the fruit of his conquest, for he lost his life there.

In the same way, if one had to decide whether soldiers should be lavishly and sumptuously dressed or armed only as the immediate task requires, the argument for the first might run as follows — and Sertorius, Philopoemen, Brutus, Caesar, and others held this view: that fine attire inflames a soldier's courage and is a spur to him; and that it also makes him fight more stubbornly, since his arms are in effect his estate and his whole inheritance to defend. This is why, says Xenophon, the men of Asia carried their wives and concubines, with their best jewels and richest possessions, with them to the wars. But the arguments would line up just as readily on the other side: that a general ought to reduce, not enlarge, his men's anxiety about saving themselves; that fine equipment makes them doubly afraid to risk their persons, and serves as a double temptation to the enemy to fight more resolutely where such booty and rich spoils are to be had. The thing was famously observed in earlier times as a powerful incentive to the Romans against the Samnites. Antiochus, showing Hannibal the army he had raised — marvellously splendid and rich in every kind of equipage — asked him whether the Romans would be satisfied with that army. "Satisfied?" replied Hannibal. "Yes, no doubt — however great their greed." Lycurgus not only forbade his soldiers all manner of finery in their gear but also forbade them to strip the enemies they defeated, because he wanted, as he said, poverty and frugality to shine alongside the rest of the battle.

At sieges and on other occasions where we come up close to the enemy, we readily let our men taunt, abuse, and revile him with every kind of injurious language. There is some colour of reason in this: it is no small thing to strip them of all hope of mercy or terms by reminding them that no quarter is to be expected from an enemy they have provoked so far, and that no remedy is left except victory. And yet Vitellius found himself fooled by this approach. He had to deal with Otho's soldiers, who were weaker in valour, long unused to war and softened by the pleasures of Rome. He stung them at last with so much abuse — reproaching them with cowardice and with regret for the mistresses and entertainments they had left behind in the city — that he inspired them with a resolution no exhortation could have produced, and made them fall upon him with a fury their own captains had been unable to rouse in them. And indeed, when the injuries cut to the quick, it can easily happen that the man who was going reluctantly to fight on his prince's behalf will pitch in with another kind of spirit when the quarrel becomes his own.

Considering how important it is to keep the general of an army alive, and that the enemy's whole aim is directed straight at the head on which all the rest depend, the course taken by so many great captains — changing their dress and disguising themselves just before engaging — seems past dispute. And yet the inconvenience a man runs into by doing so is no less than the one he thinks to avoid. The captain, hidden from the recognition of his own men, no longer has the courage his presence and example would have inspired in them; not seeing the familiar marks and ensigns of their leader, they soon conclude that either he is dead or, despairing of the business, has gone off to look after himself. And experience shows both methods have succeeded and failed. What happened to Pyrrhus in the battle he fought against the Consul Levinus in Italy will serve to illustrate both points. By hiding himself in Megacles's armour and giving Megacles his own, he undoubtedly saved his life — but by that very means he came very close to the other disaster of losing the battle. Alexander, Caesar, and Lucullus loved to be recognisable in a fight by rich equipment and armour of a particular gleam and colour. Agis, Agesilaus, and that great Gilippus, on the contrary, used to fight without any display, with no imperial escort or distinguishing marks.

Among the other faults laid to Pompey's charge at Pharsalia, he is reproached for keeping his army standing still to receive the enemy's charge — "because by doing so" (I will here lift Plutarch's own words, which are better than mine) "he deprived himself of the violent impact that running adds to the first shock of arms, and he prevented that crash of the combatants into one another that usually gives them greater impetuosity and fury, especially when they rush in with full force, their courage rising with the shouts and the run. He chilled the soldiers' ardour, as it were, and made it more reserved." That is what Plutarch says. But if Caesar had come off worse, why might not someone else have argued the reverse — that the strongest and steadiest fighting stance is one in which a man is planted firm, without motion; that those who hold steady on the march, closing up and reserving their strength for the moment of action, have a great advantage over men who are disordered, who have already spent half their breath running headlong into the charge. Besides, an army is a body made up of so many individual members that it is impossible for it to move at that pace without breaking the order of battle, and without the leading men being engaged before their comrades can come up to help them. In that unnatural battle between the two Persian brothers, the Lacedaemonian Clearchus, who commanded the Greeks on Cyrus's side, led them on softly and without haste toward the charge, but when they were within fifty paces he hurled them on at full speed, hoping in so short a run to keep order and save their wind and at the same time to give weight and impetus both to their persons and to their missile weapons. Others have settled the question for their own armies this way: if your enemy comes at you full tilt, stand firm to receive him; if he stands still to receive you, charge him full tilt.

When the Emperor Charles V invaded Provence, King Francis had to choose between going to meet him in Italy or waiting for him on his own ground. He weighed how much it mattered to keep his own territory intact and free from the troubles of war, so that, with its resources unspent, it could go on supplying men and money as needed; and that war requires constantly laying waste the country before you, which is not something easily done at home. Add to this that country people swallow such damage less easily from their own side than from an enemy, so that mutinies and uprisings could be sparked among us; that the licence of pillage and plunder, intolerable at home, is a great relief and refreshment from the strains and miseries of war; that a man who has nothing to look forward to but his bare pay will hardly be kept from running home when he is two steps from his wife and his own door; that the man who lays the cloth always pays for the feast; that there is more alacrity in attacking than in defending; and that the shock of a lost battle in one's own bowels is so violent it threatens to throw the whole body out of joint, no passion being as contagious as fear, none so readily believed, none so suddenly spread; and that cities hearing this tempest rattling at their gates, taking in their captains and soldiers still panting and trembling, would be in danger, in the heat and rush of the moment, of throwing themselves at some rash resolution. Yet despite all this, he chose to recall the forces he had beyond the mountains and let the enemy come to him. For he could, on the other hand, suppose that being at home and among friends, he could not fail of every kind of convenience; the rivers and passes were at his disposal and could bring him supplies and money in safety, with no trouble of convoy; he would find his subjects all the more devoted to him the closer the danger pressed; with so many cities and barriers behind him to secure him, it would be in his power to dictate the time and place of battle to suit himself; and if he chose to delay, then quietly and at his ease he could watch his enemy founder and defeat himself with the difficulties he was bound to encounter — engaged in hostile country, with war made on him from in front, from behind, and from every side; no way to refresh himself or expand his quarters should disease set in; nowhere safe to lodge his wounded; no money and no provisions except at the point of the lance; no leisure to rest and catch his breath; no knowledge of the country or the roads to keep him safe from ambushes and surprises; and in case of a lost battle, no possible way of saving the remnants. And there are plenty of examples for either course.

Scipio thought it much better to attack his enemy's territory in Africa than to stay at home defending his own and fighting Hannibal in Italy, and it worked out well for him. But in the same war, on the other hand, Hannibal ruined himself by giving up the conquest of a foreign country to go and defend his own. The Athenians, leaving the enemy in their own territory to cross into Sicily, were not favoured by fortune in that plan; but Agathocles, king of Syracuse, found her favourable when he crossed into Africa and left the war behind at home.

From such examples we usually conclude, and with some reason, that events, especially in war, mostly depend on fortune, who will not be governed by, nor submit to, human reasoning and prudence — as the poet has it:

"Et male consultis pretium est: prudentia fallit Nec fortune probat causas, sequiturque merentes, Sed vaga per cunctos nullo discrimine fertur. Scilicet est aliud, quod nos cogatque regatque Majus, et in proprias ducat mortalia leges."

["And there is value in ill counsel: prudence deceives: nor does fortune inquire into causes, nor aid the most deserving, but turns hither and thither without discrimination. Indeed there is a greater power which directs and rules us, and brings mortal affairs under its own laws."--Manilius, iv. 95.]

But, to take the matter properly, it would seem that our deliberations and decisions depend just as much on fortune as anything else we do, and that she catches our reasoning too up in her uncertainty and confusion. "We argue rashly and at a venture," says Timaeus in Plato, "because, like us, our reasoning shares heavily in the rashness of chance."
